chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from al-Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn Asbat, from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him), who said:

I heard him (peace be upon him) saying: 'The option of return (khiyar) in animals is three days for the buyer, and in non-animals it is that they separate, and 'ahdath al-sanah' (sudden defects) are returned after one year.'

I asked: 'And what are 'ahdath al-sanah'?' He said: 'Madness, leprosy, vitiligo, and qaran (a specific defect). So whoever buys and these defects occur in it, the ruling is that he returns it to its owner until the completion of the year from the day he bought it.'

key_terms.أَحْدَاثُ السَّنَةِ: Sudden defects occurring within a year
key_terms.الْخِيَارُ: Option of return (right to cancel a sale)
key_terms.الْقَرَنُ: A specific defect (often interpreted as a disease or physical flaw)

ai.seo_question: What are the rules for returning defective goods in Shia Islamic jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Transmitted through the chain of Imam al-Rida (AS), this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* distinguishes between the standard three-day 'khiyar al-hayawan' for livestock and the extended one-year period for latent, sudden defects ('ahdath al-sanah') such as madness or leprosy. This ruling reflects the Shia juristic emphasis on protecting buyers from unforeseen deterioration that renders the commodity fundamentally different from what was sold, ensuring fairness in market transactions.
